prediction_question: For an enterprise agreement approval application lodged with the Fair Work Commission (FWC) - published in the FWC 'Agreements in progress' list about 2 business days after lodgement, with agreement title, industry and application type visible - will the Commission approve it within a fixed window of lodgement (e.g. the 21-day standard timeframe; the publisher's own statistics report a 15-day median for 2021-22 approvals) rather than later? Prospective users: employers, unions and bargaining consultants timing pay-increase commencement (agreements start 7 days after approval unless a later date is set) and IR researchers studying administrative approval friction. A useful prediction prices the delay at lodgement instead of waiting the ~2-6 weeks for the decision.
prediction_time: Instant = the application's publication in the FWC 'Agreements in progress' list (per the publisher: 'When you apply to us to approve an enterprise agreement or a section 210 variation... we add details to Agreements in progress. This is usually 2 business days after we receive the application.'). Features visible then: agreement title, industry, application type (new approval vs s.210 variation), status. The approval decision is published later - the agreement register records an approval date, and FWC statistics report approval-time distributions, so the outcome cannot exist at the instant. NOT ASSESSED beyond structure: the licence veto (class D) came first, and no historical archive of the in-progress list was verified.
target_definition: Binary on approval latency: 1 if approval date is within N days of lodgement (N fixed from the measured latency distribution), 0 if later; withdrawn/refused applications would be censored, not negative. Label source: approval date and lodgement date in the FWC bulk agreement Excel lists. POPULATION CAVEAT measured at discovery: the bulk lists are the approved-agreements register ('Search by agreement title to find all agreements approved by the Fair Work Commission'); the in-progress list is live-only; refused/withdrawn applications surface only through decision records. A duration task built from the bulk lists alone is therefore conditioned on eventual approval (survivorship) unless non-approved applications are recovered from decisions - a design problem for any reopening, on top of the licence blocker.

rejection_reason: Licence class D: the FWC site copyright for these materials permits reproduction 'in unaltered form only (retaining this notice) for your personal, non-commercial use or use within your organisation' and reserves 'all other rights'; the publisher's CC review is explicitly 'progressive' and the dataset's own page carries no licence marking; data.gov.au has no open FWC per-agreement dataset (only an 'Other (unpublished)' aggregate record). A derived, publicly redistributed benchmark is not permitted by the only instrument that governs this register. What would reopen it: (a) FWC completes its stated CC review for these materials or otherwise marks the agreement lists with a Creative Commons licence; (b) FWC or another Commonwealth agency publishes the per-agreement register on an open channel (e.g. data.gov.au under CC BY); (c) a statutory right (e.g. a specific authorisation obtained in writing from FWC). The task design (approval-latency prediction at the in-progress publication instant) and the population caveat are recorded for any reopening.
review: DROPPED on licence (2026-10-29), first discovery pass; no novelty search run because the licence veto is cheaper and decisive. Contracts at close: (1) Redistribution FAILED - class D instrument quoted above; no alternative open channel found in a bounded sweep. (2) Prediction timing SUPPORTED in structure only (in-progress publication ~2 business days after lodgement; approval published later) - no historical archive of the in-progress list verified. (3) Target obtainable in principle with a measured survivorship caveat: bulk lists cover approved agreements only; refusals/withdrawals need decision records. (4) Split capacity UNMEASURED (licence veto first); volume signals ample. (5) Contribution UNMEASURED - no novelty search; note the bench already carries one regulatory duration task (ns-bwa-advisory-lift-duration, packaged) as a family comparator, and IR economists study WAD aggregates, so a reopened lead must run check-novelty.py before any ready claim.
next_action: Closed. Reopen ONLY if FWC publishes these materials under an open licence (their stated progressive CC review, or an open channel such as data.gov.au), or a written authorisation is obtained. On reopening, next probes in cost order: (1) re-read the instrument for the specific material; (2) measure the latency distribution and per-year counts from the bulk Excel (on a worker - the all-years file was not size-probed and the coordinator must not download it); (3) resolve the survivorship caveat by sampling decision records for refused/withdrawn applications; (4) run check-novelty.py. Do not generalize this rejection beyond FWC website material.
licence_note: Class D: the only bulk channel for the register is FWC website material under an all-rights-reserved copyright (unaltered form only; personal, non-commercial or intra-organisational use only); the publisher states a CC review is 'progressive' (not done) and the dataset page carries no CC marking; no open mirror channel exists. Scope: this rejection is about FWC's website material and does not generalize to other Commonwealth agencies, several of which publish under CC BY on data.gov.au.
